q: Should I give water to my 3-month-old baby?
paraphrases: Can a baby under 6 months drink water?
It is hot, does my 2-month-old need water?
a: No. Breast milk is about 90% water, so a baby who is exclusively breastfed does not need any water, even in hot weather, until 6 months. Giving water fills the small stomach, reduces breastfeeding and can bring germs that cause diarrhoea. Breastfeed more often when it is hot. From 6 months, offer small sips of clean, boiled water with meals.

q: How often and how much should a 6 to 8 month old baby eat?
paraphrases: How many meals does a 7-month-old need?
Feeding schedule for a baby aged 6-8 months
a: At 6 to 8 months, give 2 to 3 meals a day plus 1 to 2 snacks, and keep breastfeeding on demand. Start with 2 to 3 spoonfuls per meal and slowly increase to about half a 250 ml cup by 8 months. Food should be thick and mashed, like thick porridge or mashed sweet potato with beans. Add a little oil, and include an egg, ground small fish or mashed beans each day.

q: How much should a child aged 12 to 23 months eat?
paraphrases: How many meals for a one-year-old?
My child is 18 months, how much food do they need?
a: From 12 to 23 months, give 3 to 4 meals a day of family food, about three-quarters to one full 250 ml cup each time, plus 1 to 2 nutritious snacks, and continue breastfeeding. Chop or mash food so it is easy to eat. Each day include a staple, a protein food (beans, eggs, fish, milk or meat), and vegetables or fruit, with a little oil.

q: How should I feed my child aged 2 to 5 years?
paraphrases: What should a 3-year-old eat each day?
Feeding a preschool child
a: Children aged 2 to 5 years should eat 3 meals and 2 healthy snacks a day from the family pot, served on their own plate so you can see how much they eat. Each meal should have an energy food (sorghum, maize, potatoes, rice, bananas), a body-building food (beans, peas, eggs, milk, fish, meat) and vegetables or fruit. Give milk or ikivuguto if available, and avoid sweets, sodas and too much tea.

q: What texture of food should my baby eat at each age?
paraphrases: When can my baby eat lumpy food?
a: At 6 months, give smooth, thick, mashed foods. By 8 months, give mashed foods with soft lumps and soft finger foods like pieces of ripe banana or avocado. From 9 to 11 months, give finely chopped family foods. By 12 months, most children can eat the family's food, chopped into small pieces. Moving to thicker textures on time helps the child learn to chew.

q: Can I give an egg to my 6-month-old baby?
paraphrases: When can babies start eating eggs?
Is egg safe for a 7 month old?
a: Yes. Whole eggs can be given from 6 months. Cook the egg completely until the yolk is firm, then mash it and mix it with porridge, sweet potato or a little breast milk. Eggs are cheap and rich in protein, vitamin A and other nutrients that help children grow. An egg a day is a very good habit for young children.

q: When can my baby start eating meat and fish?
paraphrases: Can a baby eat small fish?
At what age can I give my baby meat?
a: From 6 months. Animal foods such as meat, liver, fish and small dried fish (isambaza, indagara) are the best sources of iron and zinc for babies. Cook them well and mash, mince or grind them into powder so they are easy to swallow, then mix them into porridge or vegetables. Remove all fish bones, or grind small fish completely.

q: When can my child drink cow's milk?
paraphrases: Can I give cow's milk to a 7-month-old?
Is cow milk good for babies?
a: Before 12 months, breast milk should remain the main drink; small amounts of boiled cow's milk can be used in porridge from 6 months. From 12 months, children can drink boiled or pasteurised cow's milk or ikivuguto as part of their diet. Milk is a good source of protein and calcium, but it should not replace meals or breastfeeding.

q: Should I add salt or sugar to my baby's food?
paraphrases: Can I put sugar in my baby's porridge?
a: Do not add salt or sugar to food for babies under 12 months. Their kidneys cannot handle much salt, and sugar teaches them to like sweet foods and harms the teeth. To make porridge tastier, add mashed ripe banana or papaya, or milk. For older children eating family food, use a small amount of iodised salt.

q: What are good finger foods for a baby?
paraphrases: What can my 9 month old pick up and eat?
a: From about 8 months, babies enjoy feeding themselves. Good finger foods are soft pieces of ripe banana, avocado, papaya, well-cooked sweet potato, carrot or potato, pieces of boiled egg, and small pieces of soft chapati. Always stay with the baby while they eat. Avoid hard, small, round foods like whole groundnuts, which can cause choking.

q: How do I know if my baby is hungry or full?
paraphrases: Signs that my baby has had enough food
a: A hungry baby opens their mouth, leans towards the spoon, reaches for food or gets excited when they see it. A full baby turns their head away, closes their mouth, pushes food away or plays with it. Follow these signs: offer food patiently and encourage, but never force-feed. If your child often refuses food or is losing weight, see the health worker.

q: How should I feed my child when they are sick?
paraphrases: My child has a fever, should I stop feeding?
Feeding during illness
a: Keep feeding. Breastfeed more often, and offer small amounts of soft, favourite foods frequently, like porridge, mashed banana or soup with beans. Give extra fluids. Sick children need food to fight the illness. After the illness, give one extra meal a day for at least two weeks to help the child catch up. If the child cannot eat or drink at all, go to the health centre.

q: Can I give tea to my young child?
paraphrases: Is tea with milk okay for a toddler?
Can my 1 year old drink tea?
a: It is best not to give tea or coffee to young children. Tea fills the stomach without giving much nutrition, and it reduces the iron the body takes from food, which can lead to anaemia. If older children drink tea, give it between meals, not with food. Better drinks are breast milk, clean water and milk or ikivuguto.

q: Are juice and soda good for children?
paraphrases: Can I give Fanta to my child?
a: No. Sodas, sweet juice drinks and other sugary drinks give sugar without nutrition, spoil the appetite for real food and damage teeth. Give whole fruits like orange, mango, papaya or passion fruit instead of juice. The best drinks for young children are breast milk, clean water and milk.

q: Can I keep my baby's leftover porridge for later?
paraphrases: How long can cooked baby food stay?
Is it safe to give yesterday's porridge to my baby?
a: Cooked food goes bad quickly in warm weather. Feed babies freshly cooked food when you can, and throw away food that has been sitting out for more than about 2 hours, or food the baby has already eaten from. If you must keep food, cover it, keep it cool, and reheat it until it is very hot all the way through, then let it cool before feeding. Never give food that smells sour.

q: Should my child eat from the family plate or their own plate?
paraphrases: Is it okay for my toddler to share a plate with siblings?
a: Give young children their own plate or bowl. When children share, the youngest often eats less because older children eat faster, and you cannot see how much they ate. Sit with the child, help and encourage them, and make sure they finish a good portion that includes beans, egg, fish or meat, not only the staple.

q: Can babies eat beans?
paraphrases: When can my baby eat ibishyimbo?
Do beans cause stomach problems in babies?
a: Yes, from 6 months. Beans are an excellent, affordable source of protein and iron. Cook them until very soft, remove the skins if your baby is young, and mash them well. Mix them with porridge, sweet potato or rice and a little oil. Start with small amounts; a little gas is normal. Give fruit like orange or guava in the same meal to help the body absorb the iron.

q: Why should porridge for babies be thick and not watery?
paraphrases: Is thin porridge good for babies?
My baby only drinks thin igikoma, is that enough?
a: A baby's stomach is small. Thin, watery porridge fills it with water and gives very little energy, so the baby stays hungry and does not grow well. Thick porridge that stays on the spoon gives several times more energy in the same amount. Make igikoma thick, and enrich it with milk, oil, groundnut paste, egg or ground small fish.

q: Should I continue breastfeeding after my child turns one?
paraphrases: Until what age should I breastfeed?
a: Yes. Continue breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond, together with other foods. In the second year, breast milk still gives about a third of a child's energy and important protection against infections. Breastfeed after meals and when the child wants, and keep giving family foods so the child gets enough nutrients.

q: What are the food groups my child should eat every day?
paraphrases: What is dietary diversity for children?
How many food groups should a baby eat?
a: Children from 6 months should eat from at least 5 of these 8 food groups each day: 1) breast milk; 2) grains, roots and tubers (sorghum, maize, rice, potatoes, cassava, sweet potato, bananas); 3) beans, peas, groundnuts and soy; 4) milk and milk products; 5) meat, fish and liver; 6) eggs; 7) vitamin A-rich fruits and vegetables (orange sweet potato, carrots, pumpkin, mango, papaya, dodo); 8) other fruits and vegetables. More variety means better growth.

q: Is isombe good for children?
paraphrases: Can my baby eat isombe?
Is cassava leaf dish healthy for children?
a: Yes. Isombe (pounded cassava leaves) is rich in vitamin A, iron and calcium. Cassava leaves must be pounded and cooked for a long time to remove natural toxins, as is done for traditional isombe. For a baby, mash or blend well-cooked isombe and mix it with porridge, potatoes or rice. Adding groundnut paste or a little oil makes it even more nutritious.

q: Is cassava safe to give my child?
paraphrases: Can I feed my baby imyumbati?
Is cassava good for children?
a: Cassava is safe when properly prepared: peel it, soak or dry it as is traditional, and cook it well. It gives energy but very little protein, so never use plain cassava or cassava flour alone as a child's main food. Serve it with beans, groundnut paste, small fish or eggs, and vegetables like isombe or dodo.

q: How can I use small dried fish (isambaza or indagara) for my baby?
paraphrases: Are indagara good for babies?
How do I prepare small fish for a child?
a: Small dried fish are cheap and very rich in protein, calcium, iron and zinc, because the bones are eaten too. Wash and dry-roast them lightly, then grind them into a fine powder. Add one to two teaspoons of the powder to porridge, mashed potatoes or vegetables from 6 months. Store the powder in a clean, dry, closed container.

q: Is avocado good for babies?
paraphrases: When can I give avoka to my baby?
a: Yes, avocado is an excellent first food from 6 months. It is soft, easy to mash and rich in healthy fat, which gives the energy babies need to grow. Mash ripe avocado on its own, or mix it with porridge, sweet potato or banana. It is also a good snack for toddlers, for example spread on bread or eaten with boiled sweet potato.

q: Why is dodo (amaranth) good for children?
paraphrases: What nutrients are in amaranth leaves?
Is dodo healthy for babies?
a: Dodo leaves are rich in calcium, iron, vitamin C and vitamin A. Wash them well, cook them briefly with a little oil, then chop or mash them finely for babies and mix them with beans, potatoes or porridge. Serving dodo with beans and a fruit rich in vitamin C, like orange, helps the body absorb more iron.

q: Which sweet potato is better for children, orange or white?
paraphrases: Are orange sweet potatoes better?
What is special about orange-fleshed sweet potato?
a: Orange-fleshed sweet potato is better, because it is very rich in vitamin A, which white or yellow varieties have very little of. Vitamin A protects children's eyes and helps them fight infections. A small portion each day can cover much of a young child's vitamin A needs. Boil or steam it, mash it, and add a little oil to help the body use the vitamin A.

q: How can I help my child absorb more iron from beans and vegetables?
paraphrases: What helps iron absorption?
a: Iron from beans and green vegetables is absorbed better when the meal also contains vitamin C or animal food. Serve beans or dodo with a fruit like orange, guava, mango, papaya or tree tomato (ibinyomoro), or with tomatoes, and add a little meat, liver, egg or small fish when possible. Avoid giving tea or coffee with meals, because they block iron absorption.

q: Can I give groundnuts to my baby?
paraphrases: Is ubunyobwa safe for babies?
When can children eat peanuts?
a: Yes, from 6 months, but only as a smooth paste or flour, never whole. Whole groundnuts can cause choking in children under 4 years. Groundnut paste adds protein and energy to porridge, sweet potato and vegetable sauces. Introducing groundnut paste early can also lower the chance of allergy. Stop and see a health worker if the baby gets a rash, swelling or breathing problems after eating it.

q: What is sosoma porridge and is it good for babies?
paraphrases: Is sorghum-soy-maize flour good for children?
a: Sosoma is a mixed flour usually made from sorghum, soy and maize. The soy adds protein and fat, so it is more nutritious than porridge made from one cereal alone. Cook it thick, and enrich it with milk, a little oil or groundnut paste. Buy it from clean, trusted sources and store it dry to avoid mould.

q: Is ikivuguto good for children?
paraphrases: Can my child drink fermented milk?
Is ikivuguto better than fresh milk?
a: Yes. Ikivuguto (fermented milk) is rich in protein and calcium and is often easier to digest than fresh milk, which can help children recovering from diarrhoea. Make sure it is prepared from boiled or pasteurised milk in clean containers. Give it from 12 months as a drink, or mix a little into porridge for younger babies.

q: How often should my child eat liver?
paraphrases: Is liver good for babies?
a: Liver is one of the richest sources of iron and vitamin A. A small portion (about 1 to 2 tablespoons, well cooked and mashed) once or twice a week is very good for children from 6 months. Do not give large amounts every day, because liver has so much vitamin A. Chicken, goat or beef liver are all good.

q: Are cooking bananas (ibitoki) good food for children?
paraphrases: Can I feed my baby matoke?
a: Cooking bananas give energy, but like cassava they are low in protein. They are fine as the staple of a meal if you add protein and vegetables: mash cooked ibitoki with beans or groundnut sauce, small fish or egg, and green vegetables, with a little oil. Ripe sweet bananas (imineke) are a good snack on their own.

q: Which local foods are rich in iron?
paraphrases: What foods help prevent anaemia in children?
Iron-rich foods in Rwanda
a: The best sources are animal foods, because the body absorbs their iron easily: liver, red meat, small dried fish (isambaza, indagara) and eggs. Good plant sources are beans, peas, soy, sorghum, millet and dark green leaves such as dodo, isombe and pumpkin leaves. Give plant sources with a vitamin C fruit like orange, guava or tree tomato, and avoid tea with meals.

q: Which local foods are rich in calcium for strong bones?
paraphrases: What foods have calcium for children?
a: Good sources of calcium are milk, ikivuguto and yoghurt, small fish eaten with their bones (isambaza, indagara, sardines), dark green leaves like dodo and isombe, soy, and white beans. Breast milk also provides calcium. Including one of these foods every day helps children build strong bones and teeth.

q: What are cheap sources of protein for my child?
paraphrases: I can't afford meat, what protein can I give?
a: You do not need meat every day. Affordable protein foods are beans, peas, soy and soy flour, groundnut paste, eggs, small dried fish (isambaza, indagara) and milk or ikivuguto. Combining beans or peas with a cereal like sorghum, maize or rice gives better quality protein. An egg or a spoon of fish powder each day adds a lot for little cost.

q: How can a kitchen garden help my child's nutrition?
paraphrases: What should I grow in akarima k'igikoni?
a: A small kitchen garden (akarima k'igikoni) near the house gives fresh vegetables every day at low cost. Good choices are dodo, cabbage, carrots, spinach, onions, tomatoes, orange-fleshed sweet potato, beans and fruit trees like papaya or avocado. Community health workers and cooking demonstrations in your village can show you how to build one. Raising a few chickens can also provide eggs.

q: Can I give ubugali to my baby?
paraphrases: Is ubugali good for a 10 month old?
a: Yes, from about 9 months, soft ubugali (made from maize, cassava or sorghum flour) can be part of a meal. On its own it is mostly energy, so always serve it with a protein food like beans, groundnut sauce, small fish or egg, and vegetables such as isombe or dodo. Make small, soft pieces that the baby can manage.

q: Which fruits are good for young children in Rwanda?
paraphrases: What fruit can I give my baby?
a: Most local fruits are good: ripe banana, avocado, mango and papaya (rich in vitamin A), oranges, guava, passion fruit, tree tomato (ibinyomoro) and pineapple (rich in vitamin C), and watermelon. Wash them, peel or mash them for babies, and remove seeds. Give whole fruit rather than juice, at least once a day.

q: Should I use iodised salt?
paraphrases: Why is iodine important for children?
a: Yes. Use iodised salt for family cooking. Iodine is needed for a child's brain development and for a healthy pregnancy; a lack of iodine can lower intelligence and cause goitre. Only small amounts of salt are needed. Do not add salt to food for babies under 12 months, and store salt in a closed container away from heat.

q: Is soy milk good for children?
paraphrases: Can I make soy porridge for my child?
a: Soy is one of the best plant sources of protein, and soy flour in porridge (for example sosoma) is good from 6 months. Home-made soy milk can be used in porridge or given to children over 12 months, but it should not replace breast milk. Soy must be cooked well. Choose plain soy products without added sugar.

q: Make a one-day meal plan for my 7-month-old baby.
paraphrases: What can my 7 month old eat in one day?
Give me a daily menu for a baby of 7 months.
a:
Example day for a 7-month-old (keep breastfeeding on demand, day and night):
- Morning: breastfeed.
- Mid-morning meal: 3–4 spoonfuls of thick sorghum or sosoma porridge with 1 teaspoon of groundnut paste.
- Snack: a few spoonfuls of mashed ripe banana or avocado.
- Afternoon meal: 3–4 spoonfuls of mashed orange sweet potato with mashed beans and 1/2 teaspoon of oil.
- Evening: breastfeed.
This gives 2 meals and 1 snack with 5 food groups (breast milk, grains/roots, beans/nuts, vitamin A food, fruit). Add a mashed egg or fish powder a few times a week, and increase the amount slowly to half a cup per meal by 8 months.

q: Plan a day of meals for my 10-month-old.
paraphrases: Daily menu for a 10 month baby
What should my 10-month-old eat today?
a:
Example day for a 10-month-old (breastfeed on demand):
- Breakfast: 1/2 cup thick sosoma porridge cooked with milk, plus 1 teaspoon of oil.
- Snack: mashed papaya or ripe banana.
- Lunch: 1/2 cup mashed beans and potatoes with finely chopped dodo and 1 teaspoon of oil.
- Snack: avocado on a small piece of soft chapati.
- Supper: 1/2 cup mashed rice or sweet potato with a mashed boiled egg and carrot.
That is 3 meals and 2 snacks covering 7 food groups (breast milk, grains/roots, beans, milk, eggs, vitamin A vegetables, other fruit). Swap the egg for ground small fish or liver on some days.

q: Give me a daily meal plan for an 18-month-old child.
paraphrases: Menu for a toddler aged one and a half years
a:
Example day for an 18-month-old (continue breastfeeding):
- Breakfast: 3/4 cup thick sorghum porridge with milk and 1 teaspoon groundnut paste.
- Snack: one boiled egg and a piece of mango.
- Lunch: 3/4 cup rice with bean sauce, chopped isombe and a small piece of avocado.
- Snack: boiled orange sweet potato.
- Supper: 3/4 cup mashed ibitoki or potatoes with small fish (isambaza) and cabbage and carrot cooked in a little oil.
This gives 3 meals, 2 snacks and at least 6 food groups. Serve on the child's own plate and offer clean water.

q: What should a 4-year-old eat in one day?
paraphrases: Meal plan for a preschool child
a:
Example day for a 4-year-old:
- Breakfast: a cup of sosoma porridge with milk, and a banana.
- Snack: boiled sweet potato with groundnut paste.
- Lunch: ubugali or rice with beans, dodo cooked in a little oil, and avocado.
- Snack: a cup of ikivuguto or a piece of fruit like orange or papaya.
- Supper: potatoes or ibitoki with small fish or an egg, and vegetables such as cabbage and carrots.
This gives 3 meals and 2 snacks with a variety of energy, body-building and protective foods. Use iodised salt in small amounts and give clean water.

q: I only have beans, sweet potatoes and dodo at home. What can I cook for my 1-year-old today?
paraphrases: Meal ideas with beans, sweet potato and amaranth for a toddler
a:
You can make good meals with these:
- Morning: mashed sweet potato mixed with a little bean sauce.
- Midday: soft beans cooked with chopped dodo and a little oil, mashed with sweet potato.
- Evening: sweet potato and bean stew with finely chopped dodo.
If you have breast milk, keep breastfeeding; this adds a fourth food group. Beans give protein and iron, dodo gives iron and vitamin A, and orange sweet potato gives vitamin A and energy. When possible, add an egg, small fish powder, avocado, or a fruit like orange to improve the meals.

q: Make a low-cost meal plan for my 2-year-old.
paraphrases: Cheap healthy meals for a toddler
I have little money, how can I feed my 2 year old well?
a:
A low-cost day for a 2-year-old:
- Breakfast: thick sorghum or maize porridge with 1 teaspoon of groundnut paste or oil.
- Snack: a ripe banana or seasonal fruit.
- Lunch: beans with ubugali or sweet potato and dodo or isombe.
- Snack: boiled sweet potato or cassava with avocado.
- Supper: rice or potatoes with a spoon of ground small fish (isambaza) and cabbage.
Beans, small fish, groundnuts, dodo and seasonal fruit are among the cheapest nutritious foods. A kitchen garden and a few chickens for eggs can lower costs further.

q: Plan meals for my child who is recovering from moderate malnutrition.
paraphrases: My child has yellow MUAC, what meals should I give?
a:
A recovering child needs more energy and protein in small, frequent meals (5 to 6 times a day) plus breastfeeding:
- Early morning: porridge cooked with milk, with 2 teaspoons of oil or groundnut paste.
- Mid-morning: mashed avocado and banana.
- Lunch: mashed beans, rice or potatoes, dodo, and an egg, with 1 teaspoon of oil.
- Afternoon: ikivuguto or milk with a boiled sweet potato.
- Supper: ibitoki or potatoes with ground small fish and carrots.
- Before bed: a small cup of enriched porridge.
Follow any supplementary food given by the health centre, and attend all follow-up visits. Go back immediately if the child stops eating or becomes sick.

q: My child does not eat meat or fish. Can they still get a good diet?
paraphrases: Vegetarian meal plan for a child
a: Yes, with care. Give eggs and milk or ikivuguto every day if possible, because they provide protein, vitamin B12 and other nutrients found mainly in animal foods. Combine beans, peas or soy with sorghum, maize or rice for good protein. Give dark green leaves with a vitamin C fruit for iron, and add groundnut paste or avocado for energy. If the child eats no animal foods at all, discuss supplements with the health worker.

q: Is ubugali with beans a good meal for my child?
paraphrases: Is rice and beans enough for my toddler?
a: It is a good base: ubugali gives energy and beans give protein and iron. You can make it better by adding a vegetable such as dodo, isombe, cabbage or carrots, a little oil, and a fruit after the meal. Adding an egg, small fish or a little meat a few times a week makes the iron easier to absorb. Variety across the day helps more than any single meal.

q: How can I plan a week of varied meals for my toddler?
paraphrases: Weekly menu tips for a young child
a:
Rotate foods so each day covers at least 5 food groups:
- Staples: alternate sorghum porridge, rice, potatoes, sweet potato, ibitoki and ubugali.
- Protein: beans or peas most days; egg on 3 to 4 days; small fish or meat on 2 to 3 days; liver once a week; milk or ikivuguto when available.
- Vegetables: rotate dodo, isombe, cabbage, carrots, pumpkin and spinach.
- Fruits: one each day, changing with the season (banana, mango, papaya, avocado, orange, tree tomato).
Cook a big pot of beans to use over two days, and keep fish powder ready to add to meals.

q: My child refuses vegetables. How can I include them in meals?
paraphrases: My toddler won't eat greens
a: Hide and mix them: chop dodo or spinach very finely and stir it into bean sauce, porridge or mashed potato; mash carrots or pumpkin into sweet potato; and cook vegetables with a little oil and groundnut paste to make them tastier. Eat vegetables yourself in front of the child, offer them again and again (it can take 10 or more tries), and praise the child. Fruits like mango and papaya give similar vitamins while you keep trying.

q: Can you make a meal plan for my 4-month-old baby?
paraphrases: What food should I give my 5 month old?
a: A baby under 6 months needs only breast milk, no other food or water. Breastfeed on demand, at least 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, including at night. Breast milk gives all the food and water the baby needs. Start other foods at 6 months; I can then help you plan the first meals. If the baby is not gaining weight or seems hungry after feeds, see the health worker for breastfeeding support.

q: What medicine can I give my child to increase appetite?
paraphrases: Is there a syrup to make my child eat more?
Can I buy appetite stimulant for my toddler?
a: I cannot recommend medicines. Loss of appetite is often a sign of an illness such as infection, worms or malnutrition, and the cause needs to be checked. Take your child to the health centre or your community health worker. Do not buy appetite syrups or vitamins from shops without a health worker's advice. Meanwhile, offer small favourite meals often and keep breastfeeding.

q: My child has had a high fever since yesterday. What food should I give?
paraphrases: My baby has a hot body, what should I feed her?
a: Fever in a young child needs to be checked the same day, because it can be malaria, pneumonia or another infection. Take your child to the health centre or community health worker for a test now. Meanwhile, keep breastfeeding, give extra fluids and small amounts of soft food like porridge. Go immediately if the child has convulsions, is very sleepy, or cannot drink.

q: My child's feet are swollen. Is this from eating too much?
paraphrases: Why are my child's legs swollen?
My child looks fat but the feet are puffy
a: No. Swelling of both feet in a child can be a sign of severe malnutrition (kwashiorkor), even if the child looks round or fat. It is dangerous. Press your thumbs on the top of both feet for 3 seconds; if a dent stays, the child needs to be seen at the health centre today. Do not wait, and keep breastfeeding and feeding until you get there.

q: The MUAC tape showed red for my child. What should I do?
paraphrases: The community health worker said my child is in the red zone
a: Red on the MUAC tape (below 11.5 cm) means severe acute malnutrition, which is life-threatening but treatable. Take your child to the health centre today. The health worker will check for complications and an appetite test, and will usually give therapeutic food (RUTF) and medicines to use at home with weekly visits; very sick children go to hospital. Keep breastfeeding and feeding until you are seen.

q: My child has not eaten anything for two days. What should I do?
paraphrases: My toddler refuses all food for days
a: A child who refuses all food for two days needs to be checked today at the health centre, because this often means an illness or, in a thin child, severe malnutrition. Go immediately if the child also cannot drink, vomits everything, is very sleepy or has fast breathing. Meanwhile, keep breastfeeding and offer small sips of fluid and favourite soft foods.

q: Can I give my child traditional herbal medicine for malnutrition?
paraphrases: Can herbs cure malnutrition?
Should I take my malnourished child to a traditional healer?
a: Malnutrition is treated with the right food, therapeutic food when needed, and treatment of infections, which are available at the health centre. Herbal mixtures can cause diarrhoea or poisoning, and using them instead of treatment can delay care while the child gets worse. Please take the child to the health centre first. If you want to use a traditional practice, discuss it with the health worker.

q: Can you tell me if my child is malnourished?
paraphrases: Diagnose my child
Is my child malnourished? She is 2 and weighs 9 kg.
a: I cannot diagnose your child, but I can tell you what to look for. A health worker checks malnutrition by measuring the arm with a MUAC tape, weighing the child, measuring height and checking the feet for swelling. Your community health worker can do this in your village. Warning signs are a thin body, swollen feet, poor appetite, not growing, or frequent illness. If you are worried, have your child measured this week.

q: My baby is vomiting everything and has diarrhoea. What should I give?
paraphrases: My baby throws up every feed
a: A baby who vomits everything is in danger of dehydration. Go to the health centre now. On the way, keep trying to breastfeed in small amounts often, or give small sips of ORS with a spoon if you have it. Do not give medicine for vomiting or diarrhoea without a health worker. Go even faster if the baby is very sleepy, has sunken eyes or is not passing urine.

q: Should I give my child vitamin supplements from the shop?
paraphrases: Which multivitamin should my child take?
Can I give my child adult vitamins?
a: Most children get what they need from breast milk and a varied diet, plus the vitamin A capsules and deworming given at the health centre every six months. Do not give adult vitamins or extra supplements without a health worker's advice, because some vitamins and iron are harmful in large amounts. If you think your child needs supplements, ask at the health centre.

q: My child is having a seizure. What should I do?
paraphrases: My child is shaking and not responding
a: This is an emergency. Lay the child on their side on a safe surface, keep them away from hard objects, and do not put anything in their mouth. Do not give food, drink or medicine. Get the child to the nearest health facility immediately, or call for emergency help (in Rwanda, dial 912 for an ambulance). Note how long the seizure lasted to tell the health worker.

q: How many sachets of RUTF should my child eat each day?
paraphrases: What is the right dose of Plumpy'nut?
a: The daily amount of RUTF depends on your child's weight, and the health worker sets it at each visit. Give exactly the number of sachets they prescribed, spread over the day in small amounts, and offer clean water to drink with it. Keep breastfeeding. Give RUTF only to the sick child, and if you are unsure of the amount, ask the health centre or your community health worker.

q: My baby is 1 month old and has a fever. What should I feed him?
paraphrases: My newborn feels hot
a: Fever in a baby under 2 months is always a danger sign. Take your baby to the health centre or hospital immediately. Keep breastfeeding often, and keep the baby lightly dressed. Do not give any medicine or other food or drinks unless a health worker tells you to.

q: How can I lose weight quickly?
paraphrases: Give me a diet to lose 10 kg
a: I am NutriAssist-RW, and I focus on nutrition for young children (6 months to 5 years), breastfeeding, and mothers' nutrition during pregnancy and breastfeeding. For adult weight loss, please talk to a health worker or nutritionist at your health centre. I'm happy to help with feeding your children or with healthy family meals.

q: What is the capital of France?
paraphrases: Can you help me with my maths homework?
a: I can only help with child nutrition: feeding babies and young children, breastfeeding, local foods, meal plans and when to seek care for malnutrition. Please ask me something about these topics.

q: What diet should I follow for diabetes?
paraphrases: What should I eat with high blood pressure?
a: Diet for diabetes or high blood pressure depends on your health and medicines, so please get advice from a doctor or nutritionist at your health centre. I focus on nutrition for young children and for mothers during pregnancy and breastfeeding. I'm happy to help with those.

q: Should I give my newborn the first yellow milk (colostrum)?
paraphrases: Is colostrum good for the baby?
Should I throw away the first milk?
a: Yes, always. Colostrum, the thick yellow milk of the first days, is the baby's first vaccine. It is rich in antibodies and vitamin A and protects against infections. Put the baby to the breast within the first hour after birth and do not give water, sugar water or other drinks before breastfeeding. The milk will increase in the following days.

q: How do I know my baby is attached well to the breast?
paraphrases: My nipples hurt when breastfeeding
a: Signs of good attachment: the baby's mouth is wide open, the lower lip is turned out, the chin touches the breast, and more of the dark area (areola) is visible above the mouth than below. You hear slow, deep sucks and swallowing, and it does not hurt. Pain or sore nipples usually mean poor attachment; take the baby off gently and try again. A health worker or experienced mother can help.

q: How can I keep breastfeeding when I go back to work?
paraphrases: I work in the field, how can my baby get breast milk?
How do I express breast milk?
a: Express milk by hand into a clean cup before you leave, and the caregiver can give it to the baby with a clean cup (not a bottle). Expressed milk can be kept covered at room temperature for about 4 hours, or longer in a cool place or fridge. Breastfeed often when you are with the baby, including at night. If possible, take the baby with you or come home to breastfeed during the day.

q: Can I breastfeed when I am sick?
paraphrases: I have malaria, can I still breastfeed?
Can I breastfeed with a cold?
a: Yes, for most common illnesses such as a cold, flu, malaria or diarrhoea, you should continue breastfeeding. Your milk passes antibodies to the baby that help protect them. Wash your hands before feeding and rest and drink plenty. Tell the health worker you are breastfeeding when you get medicine, so they choose medicines that are safe for the baby.

q: Can a mother with HIV breastfeed?
paraphrases: I am HIV positive, should I breastfeed my baby?
a: In Rwanda, mothers living with HIV are usually advised to breastfeed while taking their HIV medicine (ART) every day, which greatly lowers the risk of passing HIV to the baby. Breastfeed only for the first 6 months, then continue with other foods as advised. The health worker will also give the baby preventive medicine and testing. Follow the advice of your health centre closely.

q: How many times a day should I breastfeed my newborn?
paraphrases: How often should a baby breastfeed?
a: Breastfeed whenever the baby wants, day and night, at least 8 to 12 times in 24 hours. Let the baby finish the first breast before offering the second. Signs the baby is getting enough are at least 6 wet nappies a day after the first week, regular stools, and steady weight gain at check-ups.

q: What should I eat while breastfeeding?
paraphrases: Diet for a breastfeeding mother
a: A breastfeeding mother needs more food: eat an extra meal or two snacks each day, with a variety of foods such as beans, eggs, milk, fish or meat, dark green vegetables, fruit and a staple. Drink water whenever you feel thirsty. Avoid alcohol and limit tea and coffee. Your diet keeps you strong, and eating well helps protect the nutrients in your milk.

q: Why should pregnant women take iron and folic acid tablets?
paraphrases: Do I need iron tablets in pregnancy?
a: Iron prevents anaemia, which makes the mother tired and increases the risk of a small or early baby. Folic acid helps prevent birth defects of the baby's brain and spine. Take the tablets every day as given at antenatal care, preferably with food and not with tea. If they upset your stomach, take them at night and tell the health worker.

q: Why is antenatal care important for my baby's nutrition?
paraphrases: How many antenatal visits should I attend?
a: Antenatal care checks the mother's weight, blood and health, gives iron and folic acid tablets, and gives advice on eating well, all of which help the baby grow well before birth. Start antenatal visits as early as possible in pregnancy and attend all visits the health centre schedules. A baby who grows well in the womb starts life with less risk of stunting.

q: Is it safe to drink alcohol during pregnancy or breastfeeding?
paraphrases: Can I drink urwagwa while pregnant?
a: No. Alcohol, including traditional beers like urwagwa and ikigage, passes to the baby through the placenta and breast milk and can harm the baby's brain and growth. There is no safe amount in pregnancy. Avoid alcohol while pregnant and breastfeeding, and choose water, milk or porridge instead.

q: When should I wash my hands to protect my child?
paraphrases: What are the key times for handwashing?
a: Wash your hands with soap and water before cooking, before feeding the child, before eating, after using the toilet, and after cleaning the child's bottom or changing nappies. Also wash the child's hands before they eat. A simple handwashing station (kandagira ukarabe) near the latrine makes it easier. Clean hands prevent diarrhoea, which is a major cause of malnutrition.

q: Why should I keep my child away from animal droppings?
paraphrases: Can chickens in the house make my child sick?
a: Animal droppings carry germs that cause diarrhoea and long-term gut damage, which stops children absorbing nutrients and can lead to stunting even if they eat well. Keep chickens and other animals out of the house and the children's play area, give children a clean mat to play on, and wash their hands often. Keep animal pens away from where food is prepared.

q: How should I make water safe for my child?
paraphrases: Do I need to boil water for my baby?
a: Boil drinking water for young children (bring it to a rolling boil), or treat it with water treatment tablets or liquid as instructed, then store it in a clean, covered container. Pour from the container instead of dipping cups into it. Clean water prevents diarrhoea and worms that cause malnutrition.

q: How often should my child be weighed?
paraphrases: Why is growth monitoring important?
a: Take your child to growth monitoring every month, held by community health workers in your village. Each visit, the child is weighed and measured and the result is marked on the growth chart in the child's health book. If the line goes flat or down, the child is not growing well, even if they look healthy. The health worker can then help early, before malnutrition becomes severe.

q: What is Shisha Kibondo?
paraphrases: Who can get Shisha Kibondo flour?
a: Shisha Kibondo is a fortified blended flour provided by the Rwandan government to help prevent stunting. It is given to eligible pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers and young children, mainly in families with low income. It is cooked as porridge. Ask your community health worker or health centre if your family is eligible, and use it for the mother or child it was given for.

q: What is igikoni cy'umudugudu?
paraphrases: What happens at the village kitchen?
a: Igikoni cy'umudugudu (the village community kitchen) is where mothers, fathers and caregivers learn to prepare nutritious meals for children using local foods, through cooking demonstrations led by community health workers and volunteers. Children with poor growth may also be fed there. It is a good place to learn recipes like enriched porridge and balanced meals. Ask your community health worker when sessions happen.

q: Does health insurance cover malnutrition treatment?
paraphrases: Do I need to pay for my child's malnutrition treatment?
a: With community-based health insurance (mutuelle de santé), care at health centres and public hospitals costs very little, and treatment of acute malnutrition is part of public health services. Make sure your family's mutuelle is up to date. Do not let cost delay care: your community health worker or the health centre can advise you on support.

q: My mother-in-law says I should give my baby water and porridge before 6 months. What should I do?
paraphrases: Family members want me to start food early
a: Thank her for caring, and explain that health workers now advise only breast milk until 6 months, because early water and porridge cause diarrhoea and reduce breast milk, while breast milk alone gives everything the baby needs. You can bring her to a health centre visit or to the community health worker so she hears it too. From 6 months, she can be a great help in preparing good meals.

q: An older sibling looks after my baby while I work. How can I make sure the baby eats well?
paraphrases: My child is cared for by others during the day
a: Prepare the baby's meals in advance and show the caregiver how much to give and how to feed patiently with a cup and spoon. Leave expressed breast milk in a clean, covered cup if the baby is young. Teach handwashing before feeding. Ask the caregiver to tell you if the baby refused food. Breastfeed often in the morning, evening and night when you are together.

q: We have little food during the lean season. How can I protect my child?
paraphrases: How do I feed my child when food is short?
a: Give young children priority for the most nutritious foods, like beans, eggs, milk and small fish, because they grow fastest and get sick most easily. Keep breastfeeding, which is free and nutritious. Make porridge thick, not watery, and add oil or groundnut paste when possible. Use wild and garden greens like dodo. Ask your community health worker about support programmes, and have the child's growth checked monthly.

q: My child eats very slowly and gets distracted. What can I do?
paraphrases: My toddler plays instead of eating
a: Sit with the child in a calm place, away from TV, phones and play, and give them their own plate. Talk to and encourage them, let them touch food and feed themselves, and give small portions they can finish. Allow enough time but end the meal after about 20 to 30 minutes, and offer a healthy snack later. Don't force-feed or punish; regular meal times help children learn to eat well.
